question: Who was Amos, in what period did he prophesy, and with what image does the book introduce the voice of the LORD?
The noun פֶּשַׁע (pesha‘, “transgression, rebellion”) opens each oracle against the nations: what kind of crimes are called this, if these peoples had not received the law of Moses?
What pattern is repeated in the oracles against Damascus, Gaza, Tyre, Edom and Ammon, and what does the formula “for three transgressions, even four” suggest?
Tyre and Edom are accused of disregarding “a covenant of brotherhood” and stifling compassion: what broken relationships in your life still call for care or repair?
What concrete practices does Amos denounce in Israel, and who are their victims?
After six neighboring nations, the oracle reaches Judah and then Israel: what effect would this order have on Israelite hearers who applauded the first condemnations?
The text recalls the נָזִיר (nazir, “Nazirite, consecrated one”) and the prophets God raised up: what does it mean that the people made the Nazirites drink wine and ordered the prophets to be silent?
God reminds Israel of what He had done for it before accusing it: what place does the memory of good received have in your decisions today?
What questions of cause and effect does Amos ask in verses 3 to 8, and to what conclusion do they lead in verse 8?
How should we understand that God's having “known” Israel among all the families is a reason for punishment, and not for security?
The word אֲרִי (’ari, “lion”) appears in the roar of verse 8 and in the shepherd who rescues pieces of a sheep: what do these two scenes say about what awaits Samaria?
The prophet speaks of winter houses, summer houses and houses of ivory: what relationship do you see between the comfort you have and justice toward others?
Whom does Amos call “cows of Bashan,” what are they accused of, and with what irony does he invite the people to go to Bethel and Gilgal?
The verb שׁוּב (shuv, “return”) forms the refrain “yet you did not return to Me”: what events precede each repetition, and what does this refrain reveal?
How should we understand the warning “prepare to meet your God” right after the list of calamities, and why is it followed by a hymn to the Creator?
What hard experiences in your life have you later perceived as a call to return to God?
What lament does Amos raise over the “Virgin Israel,” and what contrast is there between seeking the LORD and seeking Bethel, Gilgal and Beersheba?
The verb דָּרַשׁ (darash, “seek”) appears in “seek Me and live” and in “seek good”: how does the chapter relate seeking God and seeking justice?
Why did the people long for “the day of the LORD,” and why does God reject the feasts and songs of a people who went to the sanctuaries?
“Let justice roll on like a river, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream”: where would you like to see this image come true in your city or your work?
How does Amos describe the life of those “at ease in Zion” and “secure on Mount Samaria,” and what detail appears at the end of verse 6?
The adjective שַׁאֲנָן (sha’anan, “at ease, complacent”) opens the chapter's “woe”: when does ease become a problem in the prophet's eyes?
What do the questions about horses on the rocks and oxen plowing there mean, and how are they linked to justice turned into poison?
The text accuses those who live in comfort without grieving “over the ruin of Joseph”: what suffering around you risks not troubling you?
What are the three visions of this chapter, and how does Amos react to each of them?
The vision of the אֲנָךְ (’anakh, “plumb line”) uses a building tool: what does a plumb line check in a wall, and what does this suggest about what God does among His people?
How does Amaziah understand Amos's message, and how does Amos defend his own call by saying he was neither a prophet nor the son of a prophet?
Amos intercedes saying “how will Jacob survive, since he is so small?”: for whom could you intercede with this same insistence?
How does the chapter describe the merchants who wait for the New Moon and the Sabbath to end, and what frauds do they plan?
The vision of the basket of קַיִץ (qayits, “summer fruit”) makes a play of sound with קֵץ (qets, “end”): why does such an ordinary image serve to announce something so grave?
What kind of famine does the LORD announce in verses 11 and 12, and why would it be worse than a lack of bread?
The merchants keep the Sabbath hoping it will pass quickly: at what points can your religious practice coexist with a life that contradicts what it celebrates?
Where does the prophet see the Lord at the beginning of the chapter, and to what places would the fugitives try to escape without success?
What does God mean by comparing Israel with the Cushites, the Philistines and the Arameans, and how does this fit with the promise not to destroy the house of Jacob completely?
The promise speaks of raising up the fallen סֻכָּה (sukkah, “tent, booth”) of David: what image of kingdom does this word evoke, and how is the verse taken up in Acts 15?
The book ends with replanted vineyards and rebuilt cities: what hope does this image of restoration bring to something in your life that seems to be in ruins?
